utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, you may proceed to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Zecevic, that the waiver applies also for today's sitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So on my own behalf and also on behalf of my two colleagues we would like to apologise to everyone for starting with more than an hour's delay. The reason, very simply put, is that we required more time to have the two drafts prepared and vetted. We are now in a position to hand down both judgements, both decisions, and we will start with the one relative to the motion for provisional release of the accused General Talic. With your permission, I will skip the introductory part, and that includes also in the part under "Discussion," the "Applicable Law," and start with the section which has a -- as a subtitle "Application of the law to the fact." For the interpreters, starting from paragraph numbered 26, on page 7. This Trial Chamber is seized of an application by the accused Talic for provisional release on humanitarian grounds, namely on the grounds of his ill-health. The humanitarian basis makes this application distinct from most of the other applications considered and decided by this Tribunal. It is different from the cases like those of Plavsic, Gruban, Hadzihasanovic, Alagic, and Kubura, for instance, because in all of those cases provisional release was sought during the pre-trial phase and there was no critical state of health involved. It is different from the Djukic case because in that case, too, provisional release was sought in the pre-trial stage and in addition the terminal cancer condition of the accused was such as to be unequivocally incompatible with any kind of detention. It is being pointed out from the very outset, therefore, that Talic's case cannot be considered and dealt with in the same manner as that adopted by this Tribunal in any of the above-mentioned decisions and others with which this case cannot be strictly compared. Still, having heard the testimonies of the medical officer of the Detention Unit and of the two experts appointed by this Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we ask you please to slow down a little bit for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I will slow down, and I apologise. In addition to the documentation made available, there can be no doubt that Talic is suffering from an incurable and inoperable locally advanced carcinoma which presently is estimated to be at stage III-B with a rather unfavourable prognosis of survival even on short term. The Trial Chamber is of the view that Rule 65(B) is silent on the circumstances justifying provisional release, specifically to enable individual cases to be determined on their merits and by application of discretion in the interests of justice. In determining these individual cases, it is necessary to bear in mind the rationale for the institution of provisional release which is linked inevitably to the rationale for the institution of detention on remand. The Trial Chamber stresses that the rationale behind the institution of detention on remand is to ensure that the accused will be present for his or her trial. Detention on remand does not have a penal character. It is not a punishment, as the accused prior to his conviction has the benefit of the presumption of innocence. This fundamental principle is enshrined in Article 21, para 3 of the Statute, and applies at all stages of the trial, including the trial period, the trial phase. The argument of the Prosecution that it would be inappropriate for this Trial Chamber to grant Talic provisional release given the stage the trial has reached and the nature of the evidence that has been brought forward to date can only be relevant in the context of an application for provisional release insofar as it may convince the Trial Chamber that once provisionally released, Talic may try to abscond or in any way interfere with the administration of justice by posing a danger to any victim, witness, or other person. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that no evidence has been adduced to show that there are any such clear, present, or future dangers. The Trial Chamber has also considered the submissions by the Prosecution that the provisional release of Talic could be extremely damaging to the institutional authority of the Prosecutor and her ability to conduct investigations in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and the subsequent trial in The Hague. The Trial Chamber has carefully balanced two main factors, namely the public interest, including the interests of victims and witnesses who have agreed to cooperate with the Prosecution, and the right of all detainees to be treated in a humane manner according to the fundamental principles of respect for the inherent dignity and of the presumption of innocence. As a result, it is convinced that what would indeed be extremely damaging to the institutional authority of the Prosecutor and, even more so, that of this Tribunal, is if this Trial Chamber were to disregard the stark reality of Talic's medical condition and ignore the fact that this is a Tribunal created to assert, defend, and apply humanitarian law. The stark reality of Talic's medical condition is that there is no escape for him from the natural consequence that his illness will ultimately bring about, because his condition is incurable and inoperable and can only deteriorate with or without treatment. The stark reality is that the odds in favour of his being alive a year from now are few indeed. This scenario ultimately also means that it is very unlikely that Talic would be still alive when this trial comes to an end -- to its end, or more so that if found guilty, he would be in a position to serve any sentence. Indeed, this is the stark reality of the situation that this Trial Chamber is faced with. Yet the Prosecution continues to show concern with the fact that the victims and witnesses who have agreed to cooperate with this office will not have a favourable view of such a release and in the context of their own suffering, they will not understand the humanitarian motivation behind such a release. The Trial Chamber is certainly not insensitive to the concerns of the Prosecution and, even more so, to those of the victims and witnesses who may fail to understand, as suggested by the Prosecution. It is the duty of this Chamber, however, to emphasise that such concerns cannot form the basis of any decision of this Tribunal which would be tantamount to abdicating from its responsibility to apply humanitarian law when this is appropriate. There can be no doubt that when the medical condition of the accused is such as to become incompatible with a state of continued detention, it is the duty of this Tribunal and any court or tribunal to intervene and on the basis of humanitarian law provide the necessary remedies. In this context, the Chamber makes reference to the recent decision of the first section of the European Court of Human Rights in re Mouisel v. France, which ruled for admissibility in a case which dealt with the continued detention of a person suffering from cancer, requiring intensive treatment, involving transfer to hospital under escort as being in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention. The Trial Chamber has no doubt at all that Talic's medical condition is such as to warrant in an unequivocal manner a prompt and effective humanitarian intervention.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be inappropriate for this Trial Chamber to wait until Talic is on the verge of death before considering favourably his application for provisional release and in the meantime allow a situation to develop which would amount to what is described in the Mouisel decision supra as being an inhumane one. This is all the more so when, as stated earlier, detention on remand is not meant to serve as a punishment but only as a means to ensure the presence of the accused for the trial. The Trial Chamber, given the scenario depicted above, fails to understand the request of the Prosecution for the continued detention of Talic, knowing that before long and in all probability before this trial reaches its end, his condition will not be any different from Djukic and would, as in that case, necessitate a practically unconditional provisional release. The Trial Chamber believes that given the medical condition of Talic, it would be unjust and inhumane to prolong his detention on remand until he is half dead before releasing him, basing itself on the medical reports and the testimony of the medical doctors involved, the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the gravity of Talic's current state of health is not compatible with any continued detention on remand for a long period. As explained in the Mouisel case, the palliative care and treatment which Talic's condition requires and will require more in the future justifies a different environment. Moreover, it has rightly been pointed out by the warden of the Detention Unit, as well as by the Prosecution -- not by the warden. It's been the commandant -- that security and logistical problems may arise if Talic seeks to have treatment by way of chemotherapy while he remains in the custody of the Detention Unit, and even if he is given treatment for some time in a hospital in the Netherlands. The Trial Chamber, in addition, believes that for the same considerations outlined in the previous paragraphs, the suggestion of the Prosecution, namely that of providing for the continued detention of Talic at the Military Academy Hospital in Belgrade in a secure environment without the possibility of leaving that environment, instead of continuing to detain him in the Detention Unit in The Hague, is not the appropriate solution as the circumstances that necessitate the humanitarian intervention of this Tribunal would remain the same. The Tribunal, however, as stated above has no reason -- has no doubt that Talic's case cannot be treated the same way as that of Djukic, and a number of conditions attached to his release are necessary and appropriate to ensure that this ongoing trial is in no way prejudiced. One of these conditions is in line with what the Prosecution has asked, namely that this Trial Chamber agrees that until and unless otherwise decided by this Tribunal, the request by Talic to enable him to return to the municipality of Banja Luka in Republika Srpska should not be acceded to. This Chamber believes that the fact that the trial against him is ongoing justifies this measure or restriction and the Trial Chamber is further satisfied that no prejudice will be caused to him as a consequence, because in any case he will be confined to Belgrade, where he can equally have and benefit from the proximity of his family. For the same reason mentioned in the previous paragraph, namely that Talic's case cannot be treated the same as that of Djukic and a number of conditions attached to his release are necessary and appropriate to ensure that this ongoing trial is in no way prejudiced, this Trial Chamber has reached the conclusion that the circumstances are such that his ability to move freely in the city to which he will be returned will be restricted. In the course of the debate before this Trial Chamber, the possibility of confining him to a specified residence under house arrest terms and concerns was explored and debated. In this context, this Trial Chamber refers to the decision of April 3rd, 1996 of the then-President of this Tribunal, Judge Antonio Cassese, in the Blaskic case, in which the notion of house arrest was considered funditus. Considering that house arrest is not a measure that is specifically dealt with by the Rules or the Statute of this Tribunal and is also not addressed by the laws of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and considering further that the notion of house arrest is more akin to the subject of non-custodial sanctions, i.e., as an alternative form of post-conviction detention, this Trial Chamber believes that it is appropriate to distinguish it from the imposition of a residence requirement. The Trial Chamber believes that the circumstances are such that the imposition of a controlled residence requirement for the time being will be sufficient. This Trial Chamber believes that such a measure would for all intents and purposes be tantamount to what would technically be classified as house arrest, at least insofar as freedom of movement is concerned and as explained in the Blaskic decision supra can still be considered as a form of detention. The Trial Chamber will also impose all those conditions which in its opinion on the one hand are necessary to ensure that Talic receives all the medical treatment he requires and, on the other hand, are appropriate in the circumstances to ensure that the requirements of Rule 65 governing provisional release are observed. Having premised all the above, the Trial Chamber next turns to examine the requirements set out in Rule 65. As a matter of procedure, the Trial Chamber before provisionally releasing Talic is required to hear from the host country. On the 13th September 2002 the Dutch authorities communicated in writing to this Trial Chamber that they have no objection to Talic being provisionally released on condition that he does not reside in the Netherlands thereafter. As to the requirement that the accused satisfies the Trial Chamber that he will reappear in the event he recovers sufficiently to resume attending trial, the Trial Chamber takes into account and attaches importance to the law of cooperation passed in April 2002 by the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This recent legislation sets out a procedure for the arrest and surrender of accused persons to the International Tribunal and obliges the organs of internal affairs to arrest such persons. Procedure of this nature did not previously exist, and the Trial Chamber accepts that the government has taken steps to lessen chances of accused evading arrest while in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In this connection, the Trial Chamber is also satisfied that the proposed level of cooperation is satisfactory. In this context, this Trial Chamber takes into consideration the guarantees provided by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As a whole it is satisfied with the assurances that have been put forward by the government of that country, in particular that the local authorities will closely monitor Talic at his residence in Belgrade. Consequently, the Trial Chamber does not identify in concreto any clear and present risk that Talic will not reappear for trial. As to the requirement that Talic if provisionally released will pose no risk to any victim, witness, or other person, the Chamber reiterates that no evidence or material has been adduced tending to prove that any clear and/or present danger of such risk exists and further notes that there is no suggestion that Talic has interfered with the administration of justice in any way whatsoever since March 14, 1999, the date when the indictment was confirmed against him. Nonetheless, in reaching its decision, this Trial Chamber has striven to minimise as much as possible any such risk in the future, especially by restricting Talic's residence to an area distant from the one where he initially sought to be returned and which is part of the territory covered by the indictment. Finally, this Trial Chamber observes that pursuant to Rule 65(C), the Trial Chamber may impose such conditions upon the release of the accused as it may determine appropriate. It is noted that Talic has consented to the imposition of any condition necessary to his provisional release. The Trial Chamber considers that the stringent conditions and restrictions imposed on Talic's personal liberty and found in the disposition below can adequately satisfy the requirements set out in the Rule. Therefore, the Trial Chamber, upon balancing all the relevant circumstances as required by Rule 65(B) and as discussed above, finds it appropriate to order that Talic should be provisionally released. In reaching its decision, the Trial Chamber has also taken into consideration Talic's offer to waive his right to be present should the proceedings against him continue. The Trial Chamber is not imposing any such condition upon him as a prerequisite for his provisional release mainly because of legal considerations but certainly acknowledges his willingness not to obstruct the continuation of the trial against him. The Prosecution seeks a stay of the decision in order to appeal against the grant of provisional release. The Defence has entered its opposition. It is, however, fit and proper, considering the Prosecution's response, that the grant of provisional release will therefore be stayed pending any appeal by the Prosecution. For the foregoing reasons, and pursuant to Rule 65 of the Rules, this Chamber hereby grants the motion and orders the provisional release of Talic on the following terms and conditions: 1. Talic shall be transported to Schiphol airport in the Netherlands by the Dutch authorities. 2. At Schiphol airport, Talic shall be provisionally released into the custody of the designated officials of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Names shall be provided in advance, and who shall accompany him for the remainder of his travel to his place of residence in Belgrade. 3. During the period of his provisional release, Talic shall abide by the following conditions and the Federal Republic shall ensure compliance with each and every one of them, and shall agree to abide and will abide by the following conditions and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia shall ensure compliance with each and every one of them: a) To reside and remain at all times at this address provided in Belgrade. For your information, there is a footnote here referring to the ex parte filing of the Defence counsel of General Talic of the 18th September. So to reside and remain at all times at the address provided in Belgrade, except for occasional visits for tests, medical treatment and therapy, as may be required to the VMA. For this purpose, his address in Belgrade will be communicated by the Registrar to the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; b) To inform the representative of the Registry at the field office in Belgrade if he leaves the address provided for tests, medical treatment and therapy in the -- in the VMA; c) Without prejudice to condition a) above, to remain within the confines of the municipality of Belgrade; d) Except when hospitalised at the VMA or when for reasons of health unable to do so, to contact once a day the local police in Belgrade which will maintain a log and report accordingly to the representative of the Registry at the field office in Belgrade at the end of each month; e) To assume responsibility for and bear all expenses necessary for his transport from Schiphol airport to Belgrade and back; f) Under no circumstances will he travel to Banja Luka or any of the other municipalities covered by the indictment unless authorised by the Trial Chamber; g) To surrender his passport to the representative of the Registry at the field office in Belgrade or to the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as required; h) To surrender his driving licence to the representative of the Registry at the field office in Belgrade or to the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as required; i) To consent to have the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia verify his presence at the address provided in Belgrade or at the VMA, as may be required; j) To consent to have a representative of the Registry at the field office in Belgrade to verify his presence at the address provided in Belgrade or at the VMA, as may be required; k) To consent to have a representative of the Registrar of the Tribunal to have access to him at any time in order to assess arrangements for his security and welfare; l) To consent to have a medical specialist appointed by the Registrar of the Tribunal to visit him once a month or as required in order to assess and report on his state of health; m) Not to have any contacts with the other co-accused in this case; n) Not to have any contacts whatsoever and in any way interfere with victims or any person who may testify at his trial or otherwise in any way interfere with the proceedings or the administration of justice; o) Not to discuss his case with anyone, including the media, other than his counsel; p) Not to occupy any official position; q) To comply strictly with any requirement by the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia necessary to enable them to comply with their obligation under the order for provisional release and their guarantees; r) To comply with any order and further orders and/or conditions the Trial Chamber may deem necessary under the circumstances; s) To return to the Tribunal at such time and on such date as the Trial Chamber may order; t) To comply strictly with any order of the Trial Chamber varying the terms of or terminating the provisional release of the accused. Requires the Dutch authorities: a) To transport Talic to Schiphol airport; b) At Schiphol airport to provisionally release him into the custody of the designated officials. I do not need to amplify on this; c) On Talic's return flight to take custody of the accused at Schiphol airport at a day and time to be determined by the Trial Chamber seized of the case; d) To transport Talic back to the Detention Unit or to another place indicated by the Trial Chamber. Requires the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to assume responsibility for: a) Transport expenses jointly and severally with Talic from Schiphol airport to his place of residence and back; b) The personal security and safety of Talic while on provisional release; c) Reporting immediately to the Registrar of the Tribunal the substance of any threats to the security of Talic, including full reports of investigations relating to such threats; d) Facilitating at the request of the Trial Chamber or of the parties any means of cooperation and communication between the parties and ensuring the confidentiality of any such communication; e) Ensuring compliance with the conditions impose on Talic by this or any future order; f) Submitting a written report to the Registrar of the Tribunal every month as to the presence of Talic and his compliance with the terms of this and any future order; g) Immediately detaining Talic should he breach any of the terms and conditions of his provisional release and reporting immediately any such breach to the Trial Chamber; h) Respecting the privacy of the Tribunal in relation to any existing or future proceedings and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia concerning Talic; i) Not issuing to Talic any passport or document enabling him to travel. Instructs the Registrar of this Tribunal: a) To consult with the Ministry of Justice of the Netherlands and the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as to the practical arrangements for Talic's release and return to Belgrade;. b) To keep Talic in custody until relative arrangements are made for his travel, unless hospitalisation is needed instead; c) To take any necessary measure to grant to Talic all the medical assistance required during the transfer from the Detention Unit to his place of residence in Belgrade; d) To communicate to the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Talic's address in Belgrade; e) To appoint a medical specialist to have access to Talic once a month or as may be required in order to assess his state of health and who will provide a written report to this Tribunal on such state of health. Requests the authorities of all states through which Talic will travel: a) To hold Talic in custody for any time he will spend in transit at the airport; b) To detain and arrest Talic pending his return to the United Nations Detention Unit should he attempt to escape. Orders that the provisional release of Talic is stayed pending an appeal by the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 65(D), (E), (F) and (G). And it's signed. There are some corrections and a properly amended version -- et cetera. Now, before we proceed with the other decision regarding the severance of the two cases, Ms. Korner -- because much depends on what you will tell us -- will Mr. Filipovic be able to come next week?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On -- not on -- he can only fly in on Tuesday, but he will be here Wednesday and Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman, do you anticipate that you will be able to finish with the cross-examination on those two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the cross-examination on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin could take up to a half a day, and I'm informed by Mr. Zecevic that his is about two days. So I don't know if it could be completed on Wednesday and Thursday. That's possible that it could, but maybe it can't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then Your Honours did say you would sit Friday to finish him. Your Honour, I think it's perfectly possible to have this completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we count on your presence on Friday should it be needed, Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can count on my presence, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to later in the -- the day, but I'll tell you now, that I will request your permission to absent myself the entirety of next week. Mr. Trbojevic is going to complete the cross-examination of Mr. Filipovic. We've already begun working on that, and we'll be prepared to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, as I take it, Mr. Filipovic can start -- or can proceed with his cross-examination on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Wednesday. He's flying in on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. He's flying in on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He has commitments which make it unable for him to return on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I understand that. We'll -- it's no use trying to force issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I, before we deal with that, I just want to say two things about the decision that Your Honours just handed down, before you move on to the next decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, I was going to ask you a question myself, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first is this: Your Honours, we were obliged under the Rules to put into our motion, our response to the motion for provisional release, the paragraph that says we wish to appeal. If we don't put it in, we have no opportunity of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours have very clearly stated and fairly the concerns that the Prosecution had, and I wish to make it absolutely clear, because it may be that it's -- it's not totally clear, with respect, from the way that the judgement has been drafted that the Prosecution at no time suggested that General Talic should remain in custody in the detention unit. They have always accepted that he should go to the hospital in Belgrade and it was just the terms under which he went. But, Your Honours, having made it very clear the concerns that we expressed and why we expressed them, we take the view that in the light of the conditions that Your Honours have imposed, we will not be seeking to appeal this decision and, therefore, General Talic can be released as soon as the arrangements can be made rather than to stay. Your Honour, the only other matter I want to raise on that is this: Your Honour mentioned that the address in Belgrade had been provided ex parte. In our submission, it should have been confidential rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's confidential, actually. In fact, it's -- it's put down as a footnote as confidential and ex parte.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But it shouldn't be in our -- it should be provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is only confidential, in fact. It is only confidential.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So it will be provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, that's all I want to say about those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So having heard what Ms. Korner has just stated, the Trial Chamber is further deciding that the decision for the provisional release will have immediate effect; in other words, it will not be stayed pending an appeal by the Prosecution, because it is understood that there is not going to be an appeal. It goes without saying that first there must be a further document from General Talic himself accepting and undertaking to comply with all the conditions that we have indicated in the judgement. I think there may be the need for the representation of the Federal Republic -- of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to undertake further to be responsible jointly and severely with Talic for the expenses involved in his return to Yugoslavia. If, however, we have the assurance here and now on your two feet, Mr. Zecevic, that we don't need to bother about this further guarantee by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that the expenses -- that your client is in a position to bear the expenses without creating any problems for this Tribunal, then I think we can rely on your word and proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may be assured that that is actually the situation, that my client will bear his costs altogether. So he doesn't require any additional guarantees by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean to say is that the additional guarantee, we will require in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: However, if you are in a position to prove that your client is in a position to fork out these expenses, bear all the relative costs, there will not be a need for -- to wait for the additional guarantee in writing from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This is what -- what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, we will give the green light for the provisional release to be executed forthwith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, you have the assurances of the Defence of General Talic that you may give the green light for his provisional release. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So be it. We will now proceed with a decision on the Prosecution's request for the severance of the two accused in this trial. With your permission, Prosecution and Defence, you will spare me the need having to read the -- and I will just read the disposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to say, if you just tell us what you've decided, I'm sure that will be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the foregoing reasons and pursuant to Rules 54 and 82 of the Rules, the Trial Chamber hereby grants the Prosecution requests and orders that the proceedings against the accused Talic hereby separated from those against the accused Brdjanin, charged under the same indictment, upon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Charged under the same indictment upon the completion of the cross-examination of the witness Muhamed Filipovic, presently testifying before the Trial Chamber. Any other business that needs to be addressed?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone, Ms. Korner, please. Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I raised yesterday and whenever I was before Your Honour the question of this publication of this report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- in the publication called Dani. I am informed - and I'm really leaving this as a matter for Your Honours - that the journalist in question received the information from a source and was unaware that these -- the information related to closed session testimony. Now, Your Honour, it is our case effectively -- we are in this position at the moment: We're not proposing to take the matter any further. The way in which the report was written was unfortunate, to say the least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- because the references to closed session testimony really gave the -- could have given a reader the impression, however he got the information, that this was a report of what was said in closed session. My instructions are that the seriousness of these matters is when it relates to a witness who has been testifying in closed session, and therefore my instructions are not on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor to pursue this matter any further. And I leave it entirely up to Your Honours. But those are my instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice and -- that there is the representative of the Embassy of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I am sorry, sir. I only notice your presence now. Had I noticed it before or had we been informed of your presence in this -- in this building before, I would have ensured that you would have been present in -- in this courtroom and not outside in the gallery. So please do accept my sincere apologies. Next time make sure that we are informed. Okay. There being no further business -- Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to make a suggestion in view of where we have found ourselves at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Might it make sense -- and I'm just asking the question really -- might it make sense -- I think we're coming back on the 6th of October after this last -- this next break. Might it make sense to schedule a Status Conference at that time so that we can kind of sit here and talk about where we go next with this case. Instead of having witnesses on that date, have a Status Conference. That's up to Your Honours. It's just a suggestion and a question. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can have a Status Conference before, between now and the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to be in the country between now and the 6th, Your Honour. That's what I was asking you earlier for permission to -- to not be in court next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it -- Mr. Trbojevic is here, of course. We could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But apart from that, apart from having Mr. Trbojevic here, in any case. What I would suggest is this, that in any case I think that as far as the initial phase is concerned, we definitely know where we stand. There are some further witnesses that were scheduled to come over and give evidence. What we can do is that we resume on the 6th, as planned, and on the 6th also, if it is -- if you are in agreement, we can have a Status Conference in addition to the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That -- that works perfectly, Your Honour. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We can have it in the courtroom. We can have it elsewhere. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I -- I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to sacrifice one hearing day for a Status Conference when -- when we are -- we've fallen -- we've fallen back by two weeks because of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, in any event, one of the things Your Honours may want to reconsider, and it's a matter for you, is this -- the ten-day gap in November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll think about that, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I must ask Your Honours to think about the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll think -- I need to be in my country for family reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I know Your Honour said -- but the extra added days will, I think, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think -- unless there are problems elsewhere, we could perhaps give that a second -- a second thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are a little bit further -- far from November now. But, anyway, is there any further business? There being no further business, the sitting is adjourned. And we will be sitting on Wednesday of next week. I can't remember whether it's in the morning or in the afternoon. I will have that checked and confirm it to you. Yes. Wednesday -- I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I asked Ms. Gustin to check that today as well today. I think it's the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 2.44 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of September, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25
